exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Sum and Product of Eigenvalues of a 2x2 Matrix

question.text: Given that $A=\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} & -3 \end{bmatrix},$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$
question.explanation:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by \begin{align} p(\lambda) &= \lambda^2-\textrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \textrm{det}(A). \end{align}

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

\begin{align} \begin{cases} \lambda_1+\lambda_2 = \textrm{tr}(A) \\ \lambda_1 \cdot \lambda_2 = \textrm{det}(A). \end{cases} \end{align}

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} \lambda_1 \cdot \lambda_2 &= \det(A) \\[5pt] &= \begin{vmatrix} 5 & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} & -3 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 5 \cdot (-3) - \sqrt{5} \cdot 2\sqrt{5} \\[5pt] &= -15-10 \\[5pt] &= -25. \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $A=\begin{bmatrix} -2\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix},$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$
question.explanation:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by \begin{align} p(\lambda) &= \lambda^2-\textrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \textrm{det}(A). \end{align}

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

\begin{align} \begin{cases} \lambda_1+\lambda_2 = \textrm{tr}(A) \\ \lambda_1 \cdot \lambda_2 = \textrm{det}(A). \end{cases} \end{align}

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} \lambda_1 \cdot \lambda_2 &= \det(A) \\[5pt] &= \begin{vmatrix} -2\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ 3 & 2 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= (-2\sqrt{2}) \cdot 2 - \sqrt{2} \cdot 3 \\[5pt] &= -4\sqrt{2}-3\sqrt{2} \\[5pt] &= -7\sqrt{2}. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix such that $\textrm{tr}(A)=-8$ and $\textrm{det}(A)=12.$ Then, $A^2=$
question.explanation:

\[ p(\lambda)=\lambda^2-\textrm{tr}(A)\lambda+\textrm{det}(A). \]

question.text: If $A=\begin{bmatrix} 3& -2 & -2 \\ 0& 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix},$ then $A^{-1}=$
question.explanation:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\textrm{det}(A-\lambda I)=0\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) &= 0 \\[5pt] \left|\begin{array}{cc} 3-\lambda & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 -\lambda & 1 \\ 0 & 2& -3-\lambda \end{array}\right| &= 0 \\[5pt] (3-\lambda) \left|\begin{array}{cc} 2-\lambda & 1 \\ 2& -3-\lambda \end{array}\right| &= 0 \\[5pt] (3-\lambda)\left( (2-\lambda)(-3-\lambda)-2\right) &= 0 \\[5pt] (3-\lambda)\left( \lambda^2+\lambda-8\right) &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^3-2\lambda^2-11\lambda+24 &=0 \end{align}

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

\begin{align} A^3-2A^2-11A+24I &= O. \end{align}

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by $A^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} A^{-1}(A^3-2A^2-11A+24I) &= O \\[3pt] A^2-2A-11I+24A^{-1} &= O \\[3pt] 24A^{-1} &= 11I+2A-A^2\\[3pt] A^{-1} &= \dfrac{11}{24}I+\dfrac{1}{12}A-\dfrac{1}{24}A^2 \end{align}

question.text: Given that $\,A=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,A^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$
question.explanation:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\textrm{det}(A-\lambda I)=0\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) &= 0 \\[5pt] \left|\begin{array}{cc} 3-\lambda & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{array}\right| &= 0 \\[5pt] (3-\lambda)(4-\lambda)-4 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2-7\lambda+8 &= 0 \end{align}

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

\begin{align} A^2-7A+8I &= O. \end{align}

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by $A^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} A^{-1}(A^2-7A+8I) &= O \\[3pt] A-7I+8A^{-1} &= O \\[3pt] A^{-1} &= \dfrac{7}{8}I-\dfrac{1}{8}A \end{align}

Therefore, $p=\dfrac{7}{8},$ $q=-\dfrac{1}{8}$ and \[ p+q=\dfrac{7}{8}+\left(-\dfrac{1}{8}\right)=\dfrac{3}{4}. \]

question.explanation:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\textrm{det}(A-\lambda I)=0\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) &= 0 \\[5pt] \left|\begin{array}{cc} 4-\lambda & -7 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 -\lambda & 0 \\ 5 & -3& 4-\lambda \end{array}\right| &= 0 \\[5pt] (1-\lambda) \left|\begin{array}{cc} 4-\lambda & 3 \\ 5 & 4-\lambda \end{array}\right| &= 0 \\[5pt] (1-\lambda)\left( (4-\lambda)^2-15\right) &= 0 \\[5pt] (1-\lambda)\left( \lambda^2-8\lambda+1\right) &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^3-9\lambda^2+9\lambda-1 &=0 \end{align}

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

\begin{align} A^3-9A^2+9A-I &= O. \end{align}

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by $A^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} A^{-1}(A^3-9A^2+9A-I) &= O \\[3pt] A^2-9A+9I-A^{-1} &= O \\[3pt] A^{-1} &= 9I-9A+A^2 \end{align}

question.text: Given that $A=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value of $p+q.$
question.explanation:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\textrm{det}(A-\lambda I)=0\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) &= 0 \\[5pt] \left|\begin{array}{cc} 2-\lambda & 3 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{array}\right| &= 0 \\[5pt] (2-\lambda)(5-\lambda)+12 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2-7\lambda+22 &= 0 \end{align}

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

\begin{align} A^2-7A+22I &= O. \end{align}

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by $A^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} A^{-1}(A^2-7A+22I) &= O \\[5pt] A-7I+22A^{-1} &= O \\[5pt] A^{-1} &= \dfrac{7}{22}I-\dfrac{1}{22}A \end{align}

Therefore, $p=\dfrac{7}{22},$ $q=-\dfrac{1}{22},$ and

\[ p+q=\dfrac{7}{22}+\left(-\dfrac{1}{22}\right)=\dfrac{3}{11}. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem

question.text: Given the matrix $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3 \end{bmatrix} $ and $\,f(x)=x^{22}-x^{20}+3x-2 \,$, find $f(A).$
question.explanation:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} p(\lambda) &= \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) \\[5pt] &= \left|\begin{array}{cc} 3-\lambda & -2 \\ 4 & -3-\lambda \end{array}\right| \\[5pt] &= (3-\lambda)(-3-\lambda)+8 \\[5pt] &= \lambda^2-1 \end{align}

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

$\:\:x^{20}$
$x^2-1\:$ $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{x^{22} \: - \: x^{20} \: + \: 3x \: - \: 2 {\phantom{|}} }$
$x^{22}$ $-$ $x^{20}$
$3x$ $-$ $2$

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as \begin{align} f(x) &= q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\[3pt] &= q(x)p(x)+(3x-2) \end{align} where $q(x) = x^{20}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

\[ f(A) = q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I). \]

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

\begin{align} f(A) &= q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I) \\[5pt] &= q(A)\cdot O+(3A-2I) \\[5pt] &= 3A-2I \\[5pt] &=3\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3 \end{bmatrix} - 2\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & -6 \\ 12 & -9 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -6 \\ 12 & -11 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

question.text: Given the matrix $\, A = \begin{bmatrix} 14 & 8 \\ -24 & -14 \end{bmatrix} $ and $f(x)=x^{12}-4x^{10}+x^3-2x-3$, find $f(A).$
question.explanation:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$: \begin{align} p(\lambda) &= \det(A-\lambda I) \\[5pt] &= \left|\begin{array}{cc} 14-\lambda & 8 \\ -24 & -14-\lambda \end{array}\right| \\[5pt] &= (14-\lambda)(-14-\lambda)+192 \\[5pt] &= \lambda^2-4 \end{align}

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

$\:\:x^{10}$ $+$ $x$
$x^2-4\:$ $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{x^{12} - 4x^{10} + x^3 - 2x - 3 {\phantom{|}} }$
$x^{12}$ $\!\!\!\!-$ $\!\!\!\!4x^{10}$
$x^3\!\!\!\!\!\!$ $-\!\!$ $\!\!2x$ $\!\!\!\!\!-$ $\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!3$
$x^3\!\!\!\!\!\!$ $-\!\!$ $\!\!4x$
$\!\!2x$ $\!\!\!\!\!-$ $\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!3$

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as \begin{align} f(x) &= q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\[3pt] &= q(x)p(x)+(2x-3) \end{align} where $q(x) = x^{10}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have \[ f(A) = q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I). \]

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, \begin{align} f(A) &= q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I) \\[5pt] &= q(A)\cdot O+(2A-3I) \\[5pt] &= 2A-3I \\[5pt] &=2\begin{bmatrix} 14 & 8 \\ -24 & -14 \end{bmatrix} - 3\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 28 & 16 \\ -48 & -28 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 25 & 16 \\ -48 & -31 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

question.text: Given the matrix $\, A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6 \end{bmatrix} $ and $f(x)=x^{15}-3x^{13}+x^3-5x+6$, find $f(A).$
question.explanation:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$: \begin{align} p(\lambda) &= \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) \\[5pt] &= \left|\begin{array}{cc} 6-\lambda & 11 \\ -3 & -6-\lambda \end{array}\right| \\[5pt] &= (6-\lambda)(-6-\lambda)+33 \\[5pt] &= \lambda^2-3 \end{align}

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

$\:\:x^{13}$ $+$ $x$
$x^2-3\:$ $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{x^{15} - 3x^{13} + x^3 - 5x + 6 {\phantom{|}} }$
$x^{15}$ $\!\!\!\!-$ $\!\!\!\!3x^{13}$
$x^3\!\!\!\!\!\!$ $-\!\!$ $\!\!5x$ $\!\!\!\!\!+$ $\!\!\!\!\!\!\!6$
$x^3\!\!\!\!\!\!$ $-\!\!$ $\!\!3x$
$-\!\!$ $\!\!2x$ $\!\!\!\!\!+$ $\!\!\!\!\!\!\!6$

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as \begin{align} f(x) &= q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\[3pt] &= q(x)p(x)+(-2x+6) \end{align} where $q(x) = x^{13}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

\[ f(A) = q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I). \]

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

\begin{align} f(A) &= q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I) \\[5pt] &= q(A)\cdot O+(-2A+6I) \\[5pt] &= -2A+6I \\[5pt] &=-2\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6 \end{bmatrix} + 6\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -12 & -22 \\ 6 & 12 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -6 & -22 \\ 6 & 18 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

question.text: Given the matrix $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4 \end{bmatrix} $ and $\,f(x)=x^{16}-4x^{14}+7x-3 \,$, find $f(A).$
question.explanation:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)\mathbin{:}$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

$\:\:x^{14}$
$x^2-4\:$ $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{x^{16} \: - \: 4x^{14} \: + \: 7x \: - \: 3 {\phantom{|}} }$
$x^{16}$ $-$ $4x^{14}$
$7x$ $-$ $3$

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as \begin{align} f(x) &= q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\[3pt] &= q(x)p(x)+(7x-3) \end{align} where $q(x) = x^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

\[ f(A) = q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I). \]

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

\begin{align} f(A) &= q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\[5pt] &= q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\[5pt] &= 7A-3I \\[5pt] &=7\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4 \end{bmatrix} - 3\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

question.text: If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ with characteristic polynomial $p(x)=x^2 - x - 20,$ then $A^3=$
question.explanation:
First, let's divide the polynomial $f(x)=x^3$ by characteristic polynomial $p(x)=x^2 - x - 20,$ using long division:

$\:\:x$ $+$ $1$
$x^2 - x - 20\:$ $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{x^3 {\phantom{|}\quad\qquad} }$
$x^3$ $-$ $x^2$ $-$ $20x$
$x^2$ $+$ $20x$
$x^2$ $-$ $x$ $-$ $20$
$21x$ $+$ $20$

Therefore, we can write $x^3$ as

\begin{align} x^3 &= q(x)p(x) + (21x+20), \end{align} where $q(x) = x+1.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

\[ A^3 = q(A)p(A) + (21A+20I). \]

Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

\begin{align} A^3 &= q(A)p(A)+ (21A+20I) \\[5pt] &= q(A)\cdot O+ (21A+20I) \\[5pt] &= 21A+20I. \end{align}
